seo.shortDescription: Searchable 2026 U.S. tariff table for all 120 HTS Chapter 69 lines — porcelain and ceramic tiles, toilets and sinks, porcelain and stoneware dinnerware, mugs, refractories. Base rates up to 28%, plus the extra duty by country: 10% in total on Italian and Spanish tile, 46% plus AD/CVD on Chinese tile.

overview.intro:
Chapter 69 covers fired ceramic products: refractory bricks and kiln furniture, building bricks and roofing tiles, **floor and wall tiles** (heading 6907), technical ceramics, **toilets, sinks and other sanitary ware** (6910), **porcelain and stoneware tableware** (6911–6912) and ornamental ceramics. Refractories and bricks are Free; most glazed tiles pay **8.5%** and unglazed tiles 10%, sanitary ware 5.7%–5.8%, and tableware **0.7% to 28%** depending on the body (porcelain or stoneware), the use (household or hotel ware) and the value of a standard place setting.

The U.S. imported **$7.52B** of these goods in 2025, 7.6% less than in 2024. Tiles were the largest group ($2.15B), led by **Italy** ($682M) and **Spain** ($611M); **China** ($2.05B) supplied mostly sanitary ware and dinnerware, **Mexico** ($1.23B) toilets and tiles, and **Japan** ($480M) technical ceramics.

On top of the base rate comes the **extra duty by country**. Since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff on 60 economies charges **10% in total on EU goods** (nothing is added where the base rate is already 10% or more), 12.5% in total on Japanese goods, +10% for India and the UK and +12.5% for Vietnam, Thailand and Türkiye. **China pays +12.5% plus its 2018–2019 Section 301 duty** — +25% on tiles, bricks, refractories and technical ceramics (List 3), +7.5% on most porcelain tableware and ornaments (List 4A). Chinese ceramic tile also carries **antidumping and countervailing duties** of up to 356.02% and 358.81%, and Indian tile a countervailing duty of about 3%. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico and Canada pay nothing. Dinnerware and other food-contact ware must also meet **FDA limits on lead and cadmium that leach from the glaze**.

productGroups.label: Bricks, blocks and tiles of siliceous fossil meals (kieselguhr, diatomite)
productGroups.blurb: Bricks, blocks and tiles of diatomaceous earth (kieselguhr, tripolite), used as insulation in kilns and furnaces. Free; China adds 37.5% (List 3).

productGroups.label: Refractory bricks, blocks and tiles (magnesite, alumina, silica, fireclay)
productGroups.blurb: Refractory bricks and shapes for furnaces, kilns, steel ladles and glass tanks — magnesite and magnesia-chrome, high-alumina, silica and fireclay. All Free. Magnesia carbon bricks from China and Mexico are under antidumping orders (and a countervailing duty order on China).

productGroups.label: Other refractory ceramics: crucibles, kiln furniture, nozzles, tubes, retorts
productGroups.blurb: Other refractory ceramics: crucibles, kiln furniture and setters, nozzles, stopper rods, tubes, saggers and filters. Free; Russian alumina and other refractory goods pay 35% in place of column 2.

productGroups.label: Ceramic building bricks, flooring blocks and filler tiles
productGroups.blurb: Clay building bricks (solid or hollow, including heat-insulating), flooring blocks and filler tiles. Free.

productGroups.label: Roofing tiles, chimney liners and architectural ceramics
productGroups.blurb: Clay or ceramic roofing tiles pay 13.5%; chimney pots and liners, cowls and architectural ceramics 3.2%. Both are Free under USMCA and most FTAs.

productGroups.label: Ceramic pipes, conduits and guttering
productGroups.blurb: Ceramic and vitrified-clay pipes, conduits, guttering and fittings. Free.

productGroups.label: Ceramic and porcelain floor and wall tiles, mosaics and trim
productGroups.blurb: Floor, wall and paving tiles, porcelain tiles, mosaics and finishing pieces under 3.2 cm thick. Unglazed tiles and the smallest glazed mosaics pay 10%, most glazed tiles 8.5%. The split by water absorption (porcelain is not over 0.5%) and by size is statistical. Ceramic tile from China is under antidumping and countervailing duty orders, and tile from India under a countervailing duty order.

productGroups.label: Technical and laboratory ceramics; ceramic troughs, tubs and jars
productGroups.blurb: Ceramics for laboratory, chemical and technical uses — porcelain machinery parts (Free), alumina and zirconia wear parts of Mohs 9 or harder (4%), ceramic bearings, ferrite core memories (Free), catalyst carriers and other technical ware (4%) — plus ceramic troughs, tubs and jars for agriculture and transport (4%).

productGroups.label: Ceramic toilets, sinks, washbasins, bathtubs and urinals
productGroups.blurb: Toilets (water closet bowls, one-piece and flushometer types), flush tanks, sinks and lavatories, bidets, bathtubs and urinals. Porcelain or vitreous china pays 5.8%, other ceramics 5.7%.

productGroups.label: Porcelain and china tableware, kitchenware and toilet articles
productGroups.blurb: Porcelain, china and bone china tableware, kitchenware and toilet articles. Rates run from 6% to 26%: hotel and restaurant ware 25%, dinnerware available in specified sets 26%, 8% or 6% by the value of a standard set, mugs 14%, bone china 6%–8%, other articles 20.8%, toilet articles 5.4%.

productGroups.label: Stoneware, earthenware and other ceramic tableware and kitchenware
productGroups.blurb: Stoneware, earthenware and other non-porcelain tableware and household articles. Rates run from 0.7% (coarse stoneware and Rockingham earthenware) to 28% (hotel ware): dinnerware sets 9.8% or 4.5%, mugs 10%, cups and plates above set values 4.5%, other tableware 9.8%, other household articles 6%.

productGroups.label: Statuettes, figurines, vases and other ornamental ceramics
productGroups.blurb: Statuettes, figurines, vases and other ornamental ceramics. Statues by professional sculptors and figurines of porcelain other than bone china are Free; bone china ornaments 3.3%; other ornamental ceramics 6%.

productGroups.label: Other ceramic articles (fiber-optic ferrules, slabs, other)
productGroups.blurb: Ceramic articles not covered elsewhere. Fiber-optic connector ferrules and mating sleeves of porcelain, alumina or zirconia are Free; other porcelain articles 9%, other ceramics 5.6%.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter applies only to ceramic products which have been fired after shaping: (a) Headings 6904 to 6914 apply only to such products other than those classifiable in headings 6901 to 6903; (b) Articles heated to temperatures less than 800 °C for purposes such as curing of resins, accelerating hydration reactions, or for the removal of water or other volatile components, are not considered to be fired. Such articles are excluded from Chapter 69; and (c) Ceramic articles are obtained by firing inorganic, nonmetallic materials which have been prepared and shaped previously at, in general, room temperature. Raw materials comprise, inter alia, clays, siliceous materials including fused silica, materials with a high melting point, such as oxides, carbides, nitrides, graphite or other carbon, and in some cases binders such as refractory clays or phosphates.

**Note 2.** This chapter does not cover: (a) Products of heading 2844; (b) Articles of heading 6804; (c) Articles of chapter 71 (for example, imitation jewelry); (d) Cermets of heading 8113; (e) Articles of chapter 82; (f) Electrical insulators (heading 8546) or fittings of insulating material (heading 8547); (g) Artificial teeth (heading 9021); (h) Articles of chapter 91 (for example, clocks and clock cases); (ij) Articles of chapter 94 (for example, furniture, luminaires and lighting fittings, prefabricated buildings); (k) Articles of chapter 95 (for example, toys, games and sports equipment); (l) Articles of heading 9606 (for example, buttons) or of heading 9614 (for example, smoking pipes); or (m) Articles of chapter 97 (for example, works of art).
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**1.** For the purposes of headings 6902 and 6903, the term "refractory" is applied to articles which have a pyrometric cone equivalent of at least 1500°C when heated at 60°C per hour (pyrometric cone 18). Refractory articles have special properties of strength and resistance to thermal shock and may also have, depending upon the particular uses for which designed, other special properties such as resistance to abrasion and corrosion.

**2.** For the purposes of heading 6902, a brick which contains both chromium and magnesium is classifiable according to which of those components (expressed as Cr2O3 or MgO, respectively) is the greater by weight.

**3.** For the purposes of headings 6905 and 6907, the term "tiles" does not include any article 3.2 cm or more in thickness.

**5.** For the purposes of headings 6909 through 6914: (a) The terms "porcelain," "china" and "chinaware" embrace ceramic ware (other than stoneware), whether or not glazed or decorated, having a fired white body (unless artificially colored) which will not absorb more than 0.5 percent of its weight of water and is translucent in thicknesses of several millimeters. The term "stoneware" as used in this note, embraces ceramic ware which contains clay as an essential ingredient, is not commonly white, will absorb not more than 3 percent of its weight of water, and is naturally opaque (except in very thin pieces) even when absorption is less than 0.1 percent. (b) The term "bone chinaware" embraces chinaware or porcelain the body of which contains 25 percent or more of calcined bone or tricalcium phosphate. (c) The term "earthenware" embraces ceramic ware, whether or not glazed or decorated, having a fired body which contains clay as an essential ingredient, and will absorb more than 3 percent of its weight of water. (d) The water absorption of a ceramic body shall be determined by ASTM test method designated C373 (except that test specimens may have a minimum weight of 10 g, and may have one large surface glazed).

**6.** For the purposes of headings 6911 and 6912: (a) The term "available in specified sets" embraces plates, cups, saucers and other articles principally used for preparing, serving or storing food or beverages, or food or beverage ingredients, which are sold or offered for sale in the same pattern, but no article is classifiable as being "available in specified sets" unless it is of a pattern in which at least the articles listed below in (b) of this note are sold or offered for sale. (b) If each of the following articles is sold or offered for sale in the same pattern, the classification hereunder in subheadings 6911.10.35, 6911.10.37, 6911.10.38, 6912.00.35 or 6912.00.39, of all articles of such pattern shall be governed by the aggregate value of the following articles in the quantities indicated, as determined by the appropriate customs officer under section 402 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, whether or not such articles are imported in the same shipment: 12 plates of the size nearest to 26.7 cm in maximum dimension; 12 plates of the size nearest to 15.3 cm in maximum dimension; 12 tea cups and their saucers; 12 soups of the size nearest to 17.8 cm in maximum dimension; 12 fruits of the size nearest to 12.7 cm in maximum dimension; 1 platter or chop dish of the size nearest to 38.1 cm in maximum dimension; 1 open vegetable dish or bowl of the size nearest to 25.4 cm in maximum dimension; 1 sugar of largest capacity; 1 creamer of largest capacity (each sold or offered for sale). If either soups or fruits are not sold or offered for sale, 12 cereals of the size nearest to 15.3 cm in maximum dimension, sold or offered for sale, shall be substituted therefor. (c) The percentage of water absorption of cast and jiggered ceramic articles of the same pattern, which are "available in specified sets" and which are imported together in a ratio of at least 5 jiggered articles to 1 cast article in the same shipment shall be the average water absorption of such cast and jiggered articles, of the same pattern in the shipment, which average absorption shall be deemed to be equivalent to 5 percent of the water absorption of a representative sample of such cast articles plus 95 percent of the water absorption of a representative sample of such jiggered articles.

**7.** For the purposes of headings 6911, 6912 and 6913, those provisions which classify merchandise according to the value of each "article," an article is a single tariff entity which may consist of more than one piece. For example, a vegetable dish and its cover, or a beverage pot and its lid, imported in the same shipment, constitute an article.

seo.title: HTS Chapter 69 Tariff Updates 2026: Ceramic Tile, Porcelain & Sanitary Ware Duties Since January 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 69 — ceramic and porcelain tile, toilets, dinnerware — since January 2025: the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (EU 10%, Japan 12.5%, Vietnam +12.5%), China Lists 3 and 4A, and the ceramic tile AD/CVD orders on China and India, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). **No Chapter 69 base rate changed**: all 120 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates, from Free to 28%.

Everything that changed sits on top of the base rate. In 2025 the IEEPA duties reached ceramics from every country — 15% in total for EU and Japanese goods from August 7, 2025, 19%–20% for Thailand and Vietnam, 50% for India from August 27, 25% on non-USMCA goods of Mexico, and up to 145% on Chinese goods in April–May 2025 on top of the Section 301 lists. The IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** goods of 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff**: 10% in total for the EU, 12.5% in total for Japan, +10% for India and the UK, +12.5% for Vietnam, Thailand and Türkiye. China still pays List 3 (+25%) on tiles, refractories and technical ceramics and List 4A (+7.5%) on most porcelain tableware and ornaments, plus +12.5%. **Antidumping and countervailing duty orders** on ceramic tile from China were continued on February 20, 2026, and a countervailing duty order on ceramic tile from India took effect in June 2025.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 69 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the China Section 301 List 3 and List 4A duties and their one product exclusion, Russia's rates in lieu of column 2, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. The antidumping and countervailing duty orders on ceramic tile (China, India) and magnesia carbon bricks (China, Mexico) are described in the text, with their Federal Register notices; their deposits are company-specific and are not part of the rate grids. No Chapter 69 line is on a Section 232 list or the Canada Section 338 lists. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 69 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 120 Chapter 69 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition, and no line was added, split or renumbered.

changes.title: China Section 301 Lists 3 and 4A continue after the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR announced that the 2018–2019 China Section 301 actions did not terminate on their anniversaries because domestic industries asked for them to continue. For Chapter 69 this keeps +25% (List 3) on refractories, bricks, tiles and technical ceramics and +7.5% (List 4A) on most porcelain tableware and ornamental ceramics.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duties: no Chapter 69 product listed
changes.detail: The 50% Section 338 duties on listed products of Canada took effect after a short suspension. None of the three lists in U.S. note 51(b) — nor the September 15, 2026 revisions — names a Chapter 69 subheading, so Canadian ceramics pay only the base rate and, if not USMCA-qualifying, the 10% Section 301 duty.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover all of Chapter 69
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84). No Chapter 69 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or a country exception list (note 52(j)). EU goods pay 10% in total and Japanese goods 12.5% in total — nothing extra on lines already at or above that rate. India, the UK, Malaysia +10%; Vietnam, Thailand, Türkiye +12.5%; China +12.5% on top of Lists 3 and 4A. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). No Chapter 69 line is on the Brazil exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)). From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top: 46% in total on Brazilian glazed tile.

changes.title: Third sunset review of the magnesia carbon brick orders
changes.detail: Commerce and the USITC opened the third five-year reviews of the antidumping orders on magnesia carbon bricks from China (A-570-954) and Mexico (A-201-837) and the countervailing duty order on China (C-570-955). The orders stay in force while the reviews run; revocation would remove the deposits on refractory bricks of 6902.10 (and 6815) from those countries.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still remove the base rate and the Section 301 duty on Mexican tiles and sanitary ware and on Canadian ceramics.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. No Chapter 69 subheading was on the product exemption list (9903.03.03). USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt. EU tile paid 18.5% in this period.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil, India and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Antidumping and countervailing duty orders on ceramic tile from China continued
changes.detail: After the first sunset reviews, Commerce found that revoking the orders would likely lead to dumping margins of up to 356.02% and subsidy rates of 358.81%, and the USITC found that revocation would likely lead to continued injury. The orders (A-570-108, C-570-109) continue for five more years; CBP keeps collecting cash deposits at the rates in effect at entry. They cover ceramic floor, wall, paving, porcelain and mosaic tile of 6907, and tile entered under 6905.10, 6905.90.00.50, 6914.10.80 and 6914.90.80.

changes.title: India's extra 25% IEEPA duty removed
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India (9903.01.84) from February 7, 2026. The 25% reciprocal rate on India ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75) renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025. AGOA (SPI D) makes the dutiable Chapter 69 lines that list it Free for eligible sub-Saharan countries — roofing tiles, floor and wall tiles, technical ceramics, sanitary ware and tableware. The Section 301 duty still applies to AGOA countries that are among the 60 economies. GSP (SPI A, A*, A+) remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: Scheduled: Section 301 tariff on products of Nicaragua
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that pay the column 1-general rate (that is, not entered under CAFTA-DR) will pay +10% (9903.89.01) from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028. Today Nicaragua pays the 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.58).

changes.title: China List 3 exclusion for zirconia grinding beads extended to November 9, 2026
changes.detail: USTR extended all 178 China Section 301 exclusions under 9903.88.69, among them grinding beads of yttria-stabilized zirconia (6909.11.20.00, U.S. note 20(vvv)(iii)(35)), through November 9, 2026. Matching beads skip the 25% List 3 duty but still pay the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.24) fell from +20% to +10%. It ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Composite tile ruled outside the China ceramic tile orders
changes.detail: Following the Court of International Trade's final judgment in Elysium Tiles, Inc. v. United States, Commerce amended its scope ruling and found that Elysium's composite tile is not covered by the antidumping and countervailing duty orders on ceramic tile from China. Other tile remains covered; the written scope, not the HTS number, decides coverage.

changes.title: Japan: 15% in total under the U.S.–Japan agreement
changes.detail: Executive Order 14345 set the reciprocal duty on Japanese goods at 15% in total where the base rate is lower (nothing extra at 15% or more), applied from August 7, 2025. Japanese technical ceramics paid 15%. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: De minimis suspended for all countries
changes.detail: Executive Order 14324 ended duty-free de minimis treatment for shipments of any value, origin or mode, so a single mug or figurine bought online needs an entry and pays the duty. Executive Order 14388 continued the suspension after the IEEPA ruling, and CBP's June 24, 2026 interim final rules suspended the $800 exemption indefinitely.
changes.before: Free under de minimis up to $800

changes.title: Extra 25% on products of India
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on Indian goods (9903.01.84), on top of the 25% reciprocal rate in force since August 7, 2025 (EO 14326): 50% in all on Indian tile and refractories, on top of the base rate. Ended February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Country reciprocal rates replace the 10% baseline
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 set country rates for goods entered from August 7, 2025: Thailand and Malaysia +19%, Vietnam +20%, India +25%, Türkiye +15%, the UK +10%. EU goods with a column 1 rate under 15% paid 15% in total (9903.02.20) — so Italian and Spanish tile paid 15% — and Japanese goods were later put on the same footing (EO 14345). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Extra 40% on products of Brazil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added 40% on Brazilian goods on top of the 10% reciprocal duty. No Chapter 69 line was among its exemptions, so Brazilian tile paid 58.5% in total. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Countervailing duty order on ceramic tile from India
changes.detail: Commerce issued countervailing duty order C-533-929 after the USITC found that imports threaten material injury (June 13, 2025). Cash deposits: Antiqa Minerals 3.45%, Win-Tel Ceramics 3.06%, all others 3.18%. Because the finding was threat, duties apply to entries from the date of the USITC notice. Commerce's antidumping investigation ended with a negative determination on April 23, 2025, so there is no antidumping order on Indian tile.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty cut from 125% to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14298 cut the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 10% for goods entered from May 14, 2025. A Chinese porcelain toilet then paid 5.8% + 20% + 10% = 35.8% until November 9, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Section 232 auto parts: no Chapter 69 line on the parts list
changes.detail: The Section 232 duty on automobile parts applies to the subheadings listed in U.S. note 33(g) to Chapter 99. No Chapter 69 line is listed (ceramic catalyst substrates and other technical ceramics of 6909 included), and no Chapter 69 line is on the steel, aluminum, copper, timber or medium- and heavy-duty vehicle parts lists. changes.title: China reciprocal duty raised to 125%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14266 raised the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 125% from April 10, 2025, and paused the higher country rates announced on April 2 for other countries, which never took effect. changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada

changes.title: Magnesia carbon brick orders on China and Mexico continued

They cover chemically bonded magnesia carbon bricks of at least 70% MgO, classified in 6902.10.10, 6902.10.50 and heading 6815. The 2010 orders set deposits of 57.90% for Mexico, 128.10% to 236.00% for China (antidumping) and 24.24% to 253.87% (countervailing).

changes.title: Antidumping and countervailing duty orders on ceramic tile from China

changes.title: China List 4A duty cut to 7.5%

changes.title: China List 4B suspended — porcelain sanitary ware and most stoneware tableware spared

Its Chapter 69 lines — porcelain sinks and toilets (6910.10), bone china valued not over $31.50 a dozen, porcelain steins and mugs (6911.10.15, .41, .45) and stoneware and earthenware tableware 6912.00.20–6912.00.50 — have never paid a China Section 301 list duty.

changes.title: China List 4A reaches porcelain tableware and ornamental ceramics

changes.title: China List 3 duty raised to 25%

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 69 goods were **$7.52B in 2025**, 7.6% less than the $8.14B of 2024 and well below the $9.64B peak of 2022. **Floor and wall tiles** (heading 6907) were the largest group at $2.15B — $1.43B of it porcelain-type tile with water absorption of 0.5% or less (6907.21) — followed by **sanitary ware** (6910, $1.55B), **technical ceramics** (6909, $990M) and **stoneware and earthenware tableware** (6912, $978M).

Each product has its own suppliers. Tile comes from **Italy** ($682M) and **Spain** ($611M), then Mexico ($209M), India ($143M), Brazil ($107M) and Türkiye ($81.8M); **China** shipped only about $954K of tile, because the 2020 antidumping and countervailing duty orders priced it out. China is instead the largest supplier of sanitary ware ($669M) and of stoneware tableware ($739M), and its total fell 18.8% to $2.05B. **Mexico** ($1.23B) supplies toilets and sinks ($588M), tile and refractories, mostly duty-free under USMCA. **Japan** ($480M, +6.5%) leads in technical ceramics ($345M), and **Thailand** grew 25.4% to $272M. India fell 23.8% and Türkiye 33.7%.

The figures are annual and stop at 2025, before the 2026 tariff changes (the end of the IEEPA duties in February and the Section 301 tariffs from July 24, 2026); they do not show what those changes did. Duty-collected figures are not available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Chapter 69 base rates run from Free (refractories, bricks) to 28% (stoneware hotel ware), and the extra duty **depends on where the goods come from**. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is mainly the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026: **10% in total for Italy, Spain, Germany, Portugal and the rest of the EU**, 12.5% in total for Japan, **+10% for India and the UK**, **+12.5% for Thailand, Vietnam and Türkiye**, and +37.5% for Brazil. **China adds 12.5% plus 25% (List 3)** on tiles, refractories and technical ceramics, or 7.5% (List 4A) on most porcelain tableware and ornaments. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico and Canada pay nothing. Antidumping and countervailing duties on ceramic tile from China and India and on magnesia carbon bricks from China and Mexico come on top and are not in the cells.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 69: Ceramic Tiles, Sanitary Ware & Tableware — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Ceramic Tile, Toilets & Dinnerware into the U.S.: FDA Lead Rules, AD/CVD, DOE & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 69) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What each HTS Chapter 69 line needs at U.S. entry — FDA lead and cadmium limits for ceramic dinnerware, "Not for Food Use" labels on decorative pieces, DOE water standards for toilets, AD/CVD on tile from China and India, origin marking — and the legal ways to pay less: classification, origin, USMCA, first sale, drawback, FTZ and rulings.

tariffEngineering.intro:
Most Chapter 69 goods need no license, but three sets of rules decide whether a shipment clears. **Dinnerware, mugs and other food-contact ceramics** are tested by FDA for lead and cadmium that leach from the glaze; lots over the action levels can be detained at entry. Decorative pieces that look usable for food must carry a permanent "Not for Food Use" statement. **Toilets and urinals** must meet the DOE water-use standards, and the importer counts as the manufacturer. **Ceramic tile from China and India** is under antidumping and countervailing duty orders: the importer pays cash deposits and files a non-reimbursement certificate. Every article must be marked with its country of origin.

On cost, the rate turns on facts the importer controls: whether a tile is glazed, whether tableware is porcelain or stoneware, hotel or household ware, and what a standard place setting is worth, plus the **country of origin** (10% in total for EU tile, 46% plus AD/CVD for Chinese tile). USMCA, FTAs, first-sale valuation, drawback, foreign-trade zones and binding rulings lower the bill further. Each lever depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Classify tile by glaze, size and thickness
levers.saves: Up to 1.5 points of base rate: unglazed tiles and glazed mosaics small enough to fit a 7 cm square pay 10%, most glazed tiles 8.5%; and anything 3.2 cm or more thick is not a "tile" of 6907 at all
levers.document: Product specifications: glazed or unglazed, dimensions, thickness, tiles per square meter and water absorption (statistical).
levers.caveat: Water absorption and size split the statistical suffixes, not the rate, except for small glazed mosaics. Outside the EU floor the gap is small next to the country duty, and Chinese tile pays AD/CVD whatever its line.

levers.title: Know the body, the use and the set value of tableware
levers.saves: Large gaps between lines: porcelain hotel ware pays 25% and stoneware hotel ware 28%, but household ware much less; porcelain dinnerware sets pay 26%, 8% or 6% and stoneware sets 9.8% or 4.5% depending on the value of a standard set; porcelain mugs 14%, stoneware mugs 10%
levers.appliesTo: Headings 6911 and 6912 (and porcelain or other bodies in 6909, 6910, 6913 and 6914)
levers.document: A water-absorption test (ASTM C373) and body description showing porcelain, bone china, stoneware or earthenware; the price list for the pattern's standard set (note 6(b)); the intended use (household or hotel and restaurant).
levers.caveat: Porcelain absorbs not over 0.5% water and is translucent; stoneware not over 3% and opaque; earthenware more than 3% (note 5). The set value is the aggregate of the articles listed in note 6(b), whether or not imported together, so one pattern takes one line. The declared line must match the goods; a ruling settles doubtful cases.

levers.title: Know the country of origin — and do not route tile through a third country
levers.saves: The difference between country rates: 10% in total for EU tile, 18.5% for India, 21% for Vietnam or Türkiye, 46% plus AD/CVD for China
levers.appliesTo: All lines; the gap is widest on tile, refractories and technical ceramics
levers.document: Production records showing where the article was formed and fired — the country where it was last substantially transformed.
levers.caveat: Glazing, cutting, polishing or packing a Chinese tile in another country does not take it out of the China orders: their scope covers tile minor-processed in a third country. The Section 301 duties follow the country of origin, and CBP can ask for proof.

HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20 and 52

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Mexico or Canada
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 28%) plus the 10% Section 301 duty
levers.appliesTo: All dutiable lines from Mexico and Canada — tiles, toilets and sinks, tableware
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, kept ready for CBP.
levers.caveat: The good must meet the Chapter 69 rule of origin in General Note 11. USMCA does not remove the antidumping duty on Mexican magnesia carbon bricks. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS General Note 11 (USMCA rules of origin)

levers.title: Claim AGOA or another FTA
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable lines whose Special column lists the program: AGOA (D), Korea (KR), Colombia (CO), Peru (PE), Chile (CL), Morocco (MA), CAFTA-DR (P) and the other FTA partners; the U.S.–Japan Trade Agreement (JP) on 6909.19.50
levers.document: The origin proof each program requires (a certification or declaration of origin, or the AGOA documentation) and records to back it up.
levers.caveat: An FTA removes the base rate but not the 2026 Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)); for EU-style "in total" countries such as Japan and Korea the total does not change. AGOA (D) runs to December 31, 2026. GSP (A, A*, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020, although the codes are still printed.

levers.title: Use the China List 3 exclusion for zirconia grinding beads
levers.saves: The 25% List 3 duty on Chinese grinding beads of yttria-stabilized zirconia
levers.appliesTo: 6909.11.20.00 — porcelain machinery parts, for beads matching the exclusion description
levers.document: Product specifications showing yttria-stabilized zirconia grinding beads; report 9903.88.69 instead of 9903.88.03.
levers.caveat: In effect through November 9, 2026 unless USTR extends it again. The 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.31) still applies.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 20(vvv)(iii)(35), 9903.88.69

levers.title: Check the AD/CVD scope — and ask Commerce for a scope ruling
levers.saves: The antidumping and countervailing deposits (up to 356.02% + 358.81% on Chinese tile) on a product that is outside the written scope
levers.appliesTo: Tile of 6907 (and tile entered under 6905, 6913.90.20 or 6914) from China or India; refractory bricks of 6902.10 from China or Mexico
levers.document: A scope ruling application to Commerce with the product description, composition and production process.
levers.caveat: The written scope, not the HTS number, decides coverage: Commerce found Elysium's composite tile outside the China tile orders in 2025, while tile of any size, glaze or end use stays in. Rulings take months; deposits are owed meanwhile.

levers.title: Value at the first sale for export when you buy through a middleman
levers.saves: Every ad valorem duty is charged on a lower value — the base rate and the 10%–37.5% extra duties included — when the factory price to a trading company is lower than the price you pay
levers.appliesTo: All lines bought through a trading company or agent-buyer rather than straight from the factory
levers.document: Proof that the first sale was a bona fide sale for export to the United States at arm's length: the factory invoice, contracts and payment records.
levers.caveat: Only a sale clearly destined for the U.S. qualifies, and the importer must be able to show the earlier price at entry.

levers.title: Recover duty on goods you export or destroy
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, when the imported goods (or goods made from them) are exported or destroyed
levers.appliesTo: Any line — for example tile or sanitary ware re-exported to Canada or the Caribbean
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import, manufacturing and export records.
levers.caveat: Claims have filing deadlines and record-keeping rules; check whether a given Chapter 99 or AD/CVD duty is eligible before relying on it.

levers.title: Hold, sort or kit goods in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: No duty on goods re-exported from the zone, and duty deferred until goods leave it for the U.S. market
levers.appliesTo: Any line — useful for tile and sanitary ware distributed to several countries
levers.document: Zone admission (CBP Form 214) and the zone operator's inventory records.
levers.caveat: Goods entered for U.S. consumption from a zone pay the duties in force on the entry date; goods subject to AD/CVD orders stay subject to them.

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision for U.S. goods coming back
levers.saves: All duty on U.S.-made goods returned unchanged (9801.00.10), for example unsold stock or samples sent back by a foreign distributor
levers.appliesTo: Any line, for American goods returned without having been advanced in value or improved abroad
levers.document: Proof of U.S. origin and of the export, as CBP requires for the provision.
levers.caveat: The Section 301 duties also do not apply to goods properly entered under Chapter 98, except subchapter XXIII and 9802.00.40–9802.00.80 (U.S. note 52(a)).

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Get a binding classification ruling
levers.saves: Certainty where the line decides the rate and the China list: porcelain versus stoneware, household versus hotel ware, a dinnerware set's value break, a technical ceramic (6909) versus an "other" article (6914), a tile versus a slab
levers.appliesTo: Any line where body, use, size or value decides the line
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the article, its body and water absorption, dimensions, use and value.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a changed body, design or price list may need a new one.

groups.note: Toilets and urinals must meet DOE water-use standards and be certified; sinks and lavatories need no certification. Porcelain sanitary ware (6910.10) from China pays only the 12.5% Section 301 duty.

groups.label: Porcelain and china tableware, kitchenware and toilet articles
groups.note: Food-contact porcelain must meet FDA lead and cadmium limits; decorative pieces need the 21 CFR 109.16 labels. Rates from 6% to 26% depend on bone china, hotel ware, set value and article type.

groups.label: Stoneware, earthenware and other ceramic tableware and kitchenware
groups.note: Food-contact stoneware and earthenware must meet FDA lead and cadmium limits; traditional low-fired pottery is a known risk. Most 6912 lines from China pay only the 12.5% Section 301 duty.

groups.label: Statuettes, figurines, vases and other ornamental ceramics
groups.note: Decorative ceramics that could hold food need the "Not for Food Use" labels. Ceramic tile articles of 6913.90.20 are named in the India tile order.

groups.label: Other ceramic articles (fiber-optic ferrules, slabs, other)
groups.note: 6914.10.80 and 6914.90.80 are named in the China and India ceramic tile orders, so tile or slabs entered there can owe AD/CVD.

seo.shortDescription: Answers to what people search about U.S. tariffs on ceramics: HS codes for ceramic and porcelain tile, mugs, plates, sinks, toilets and vases; tariffs on Italian and Spanish tile; anti-dumping duties on tile from China and India; and FDA lead rules for ceramic dishes.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs and import rules for ceramic tile, sanitary ware, dinnerware and other ceramic products. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Refractories and bricks are Free; most glazed tiles pay 8.5% (unglazed 10%), toilets and sinks 5.7%–5.8%, and tableware 0.7% to 28% depending on porcelain or stoneware, household or hotel use and set value.

Since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 duty is added by country: 10% in total for EU goods (Italian and Spanish tile pay 10%), 12.5% in total for Japan, +10% for India and the UK, +12.5% for Vietnam, Thailand and Türkiye.

China pays +12.5% plus List 3 (+25%) on tiles, refractories and technical ceramics or List 4A (+7.5%) on most porcelain tableware and ornaments; porcelain toilets and most stoneware tableware pay only the 12.5%.

Chinese ceramic tile also owes antidumping and countervailing duties (up to 356.02% and 358.81%), continued in February 2026; Indian tile owes a 3.06%–3.45% countervailing duty; magnesia carbon bricks from China and Mexico are also under orders.
USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico and Canada pay nothing. The IEEPA duties ended February 24, 2026 and the 10% Section 122 surcharge ended July 23, 2026.
Ceramic dishes and mugs must meet FDA lead and cadmium limits, decorative pieces need "Not for Food Use" labels, and toilets must meet DOE water-use standards.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for ceramic tiles?
searchedAs: hs code for ceramic floor tiles
faqs.answer: Ceramic floor, wall and paving tiles are heading 6907, split by water absorption: 6907.21 (not over 0.5%, porcelain-type), 6907.22 (over 0.5% up to 10%) and 6907.23 (over 10%). Glazed tiles mostly pay 8.5% (6907.2x.90 and .40); unglazed tiles and small glazed mosaics 10%. Mosaic cubes are 6907.30 and trim pieces 6907.40. Anything 3.2 cm or more thick is not a tile of 6907.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for porcelain tiles?
searchedAs: hs code for glazed porcelain tiles
hs code for polished porcelain tiles
hs code for porcelain floor tiles
faqs.answer: Porcelain tile absorbs 0.5% of its weight in water or less, so it falls in 6907.21: glazed porcelain tile larger than 7 cm is 6907.21.90 (8.5%) — suffix .11 if it fits in a 30 cm square, .51 if larger — and unglazed porcelain is 6907.21.10 (10%). Large porcelain slabs under 3.2 cm thick stay in 6907; articles 3.2 cm or more thick are not tiles of 6907 and may fall in 6914 (other ceramic articles), a heading the tile AD/CVD orders also name.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on Italian and Spanish tile?
faqs.answer: Yes. Since July 24, 2026 EU goods with a base rate under 10% pay 10% in total (9903.05.39), so Italian and Spanish glazed tile pays 10% of its value — $1,000 on $10,000 — instead of 15% from August 2025 to February 2026 and 8.5% before 2025. Unglazed tile (already 10%) pays 10%. No AD/CVD order covers EU tile. Italy shipped $682M and Spain $611M of tile in 2025.

faqs.question: Can I import ceramic tile from China, and what does it cost?
faqs.answer: You can, but it rarely pays. Chinese glazed tile owes 8.5% + 12.5% (9903.05.31) + 25% List 3 (9903.88.03) = 46%, plus cash deposits under the antidumping and countervailing duty orders of 2020, continued February 20, 2026: the China-wide antidumping rate is 356.02% and the all-others countervailing rate 358.81%. Tile glazed, cut or polished in a third country stays covered. U.S. imports of tile from China were about $954K in 2025.

faqs.question: Is there anti-dumping duty on ceramic tiles from India?
faqs.answer: There is no antidumping duty on Indian tile — Commerce found no dumping in April 2025 — but there is a countervailing (anti-subsidy) duty order since June 2025: deposits of 3.45% for Antiqa Minerals, 3.06% for Win-Tel Ceramics and 3.18% for all others, on top of the 8.5%–10% base rate and the 10% Section 301 duty. Chinese tile is under both antidumping and countervailing duty orders.

faqs.question: What is the HS code and tariff for a ceramic mug?
searchedAs: hs code for ceramic coffee mug
faqs.answer: Porcelain or china mugs are 6911.10.45.00 (14%); stoneware and other ceramic mugs 6912.00.44.00 (10%). Cups sold with saucers or as part of a dinnerware pattern can fall in the set or value lines instead. From China add 12.5% (neither mug line is on List 3 or 4A): 26.5% or 22.5%. From the EU they pay 14% or 10%. FDA limits leachable lead in mugs to 0.5 µg/mL.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for ceramic plates and dinnerware?
searchedAs: hs code for porcelain dinner plates
faqs.answer: Porcelain and bone china tableware is heading 6911; stoneware and earthenware is 6912. Patterns sold in specified sets are classed by the value of a standard set (note 6): porcelain 26% (not over $56), 8% (over $56 to $200) or 6% (over $200); stoneware 9.8% (not over $38) or 4.5%. Hotel and restaurant ware pays 25% (porcelain) or 28% (stoneware); bone china 6%–8%; coarse stoneware and Rockingham earthenware 0.7%.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a ceramic sink or toilet?
searchedAs: hs code for ceramic wash basin
faqs.answer: Ceramic sanitary ware is heading 6910: porcelain or vitreous china is 6910.10.00 (5.8%) — .05 flushometer bowls, .10 one-piece toilets, .15 flush tanks, .20 other toilet bowls, .30 sinks and lavatories, .50 other fixtures — and fireclay or other ceramics 6910.90.00 (5.7%). Plastic seats and metal fittings are classified separately.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on toilets imported into the U.S.?
faqs.answer: A porcelain toilet pays 5.8% plus the extra duty for its origin: 18.3% from China (6910.10 is on no China list, so only the 12.5% 2026 duty applies), Thailand or Vietnam, 15.8% from India, 10% from the EU, and nothing if USMCA-qualifying from Mexico. China and Mexico shipped $669M and $588M of sanitary ware in 2025. Toilets must meet the DOE 1.6 gallons-per-flush limit.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a ceramic vase or porcelain figurine?
faqs.answer: Ornamental ceramics are heading 6913: of porcelain 6913.10 (Free, or 3.3% for bone china), of other ceramics 6913.90 (6%, or Free for sculptors' work, ceramic-tile articles and Rockingham-type earthenware). From China add 20% (12.5% + 7.5% List 4A). A vase that could hold food or drink needs the FDA "Not for Food Use" labels if it is not food-safe.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for refractory bricks?
faqs.answer: Refractory bricks and shapes are heading 6902: magnesite bricks 6902.10.10, other magnesia or chrome 6902.10.50, alumina or silica bricks 6902.20.10, fireclay bricks 6902.90.10. All are Free; crucibles, kiln furniture and other refractory goods are 6903 (Free). Chinese refractories pay 37.5% extra, and magnesia carbon bricks from China and Mexico are under AD/CVD orders. Refractory cement is Chapter 38, not 69.

faqs.question: What does HTS Chapter 69 cover?
faqs.answer: Chapter 69 covers ceramic products fired after shaping: refractory bricks and goods (6901–6903), building bricks, roofing tiles and pipes (6904–6906), floor and wall tiles (6907), technical ceramics (6909), sanitary ware (6910), porcelain and other tableware (6911–6912), ornamental ceramics (6913) and other ceramic articles (6914). It excludes electrical insulators (8546), artificial teeth, ceramic toys, furniture, lamps and works of art.

faqs.question: What are the tariffs on ceramics imported into the U.S. in 2026?
faqs.answer: The base rate (Free to 28%) plus the extra duty for the country of origin: 10% in total for EU goods, 12.5% in total for Japan, +10% for India and the UK, +12.5% for Vietnam, Thailand and Türkiye, +37.5% for Brazil, and for China +12.5% plus 25% (tiles, refractories, technical ceramics) or 7.5% (most porcelain tableware and ornaments). USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico and Canada pay nothing extra. U.S. imports were $7.52B in 2025.

faqs.question: What are the FDA rules for lead in ceramic dishes?
faqs.answer: FDA detains ceramic food ware whose glaze leaches lead above its action levels: 3.0 µg/mL for plates (average of six), 2.0 for small bowls, 1.0 for large bowls, 0.5 for cups, mugs and pitchers. Cadmium limits are 0.5 and 0.25 µg/mL. Lots over the limits can be detained at entry. Decorative ware must carry a "Not for Food Use" label and a permanent statement on the base, or have a hole through it.
